blocks.text: Epidemiology counts the frequency, risk factors and burden of disease in a specified population over a specified period. Descriptive epidemiology describes disease patterns using the triad of Time (how does the pattern vary over time?), Place (how does where the population lives affect the pattern?) and Person (how do personal characteristics affect the pattern?); analytical epidemiology makes hypothesis-driven inferences from those observed associations.

Genetic epidemiology is a fast-expanding branch that evaluates inherited causes of disease in families and populations, including gene-gene and gene-environment interactions. Morton's definition: 'a science which deals with the etiology, distribution, and control of disease in groups of relatives and with inherited causes of disease in populations.'

bullets.text: Descriptive epidemiology uses Time/Place/Person to describe disease patterns; analytical epidemiology makes hypothesis-driven inferences from those associations.
Genetic epidemiology studies inherited disease causes in families/populations, incl. gene-gene and gene-environment interaction (Morton's definition).

blocks.text: Incidence = number of new cases diagnosed in a specified time interval / mid-interval population at risk (e.g. mid-2014 population for a 2014 annual incidence). Incidence is a ratio measured against time, so one-month incidence is always lower than one-year incidence.

Cohort incidence-denominator trap: if 200 of an initial 1200 at-risk people already have the illness at baseline, the correct incidence denominator for new cases over the follow-up year is 1200-200=1000 (the truly at-risk group), not the original 1200.

This standard calculation is cumulative incidence — valid in cohort studies with low attrition, but biased when attrition is significant, because dropouts are excluded from the numerator (not counted as new cases) while the denominator population still includes them.

Incidence density (incidence rate) expresses new cases per person-year of observation, avoiding the attrition problem. Its unit is time^-1 ('rather bizarre'), so incidence rate ratios (unit-free) are typically used to compare two groups.

Point prevalence = number of existing cases (new+old, minus dead/cured) at one cross-sectional observation point / cross-sectional population at that point. Period prevalence uses the same 'existing cases' numerator but assessed longitudinally over a period, divided by the mid-period population. Cases must be found at the time of observation, irrespective of when diagnosed — someone dead or cured before the observation period cannot be counted.

Prevalence = incidence x duration of illness. Chronic illnesses (e.g. schizophrenia) show higher prevalence than acute, short-lived illnesses (e.g. influenza) even when their incidence rates are comparable.

expansion: Prevalence = Incidence x Duration of illness
Increase duration (chronic illness, or reduced mortality prolonging survival) -> prevalence rises even if incidence is flat
Cut duration (a cure) -> prevalence falls even though incidence is unchanged
A preventive vaccine cuts incidence itself, so both incidence and prevalence fall

blocks.text: Worked examples of the formula's implications: a new preventive vaccine can lower both incidence and prevalence; a cure for schizophrenia would not change incidence but would lower prevalence (shorter duration); interventions that reduce mortality in chronic schizophrenia can paradoxically raise prevalence through patient longevity, without directly affecting incidence.

Migrant schizophrenia incidence 3x natives but prevalence only 1.8x: the tested explanation is a shorter illness duration in migrants (via P=I x D) — but the explanation itself flags this as 'hypothetical and not a widely established explanation'. Plausible-sounding distractors like 'better access to care for natives' or 'better treatment response in natives' are wrong; know the intended answer even though it isn't settled science.

In P = I x D calculations, a stated mortality rate is often a deliberate red herring: prevalent ('existing') cases already exclude the dead by definition, so mortality figures given in the stem should be discarded rather than subtracted when solving for duration.

Two disorders with equal incidence but differing prevalence: the tested explanation is a difference in **CHRONICITY**/duration (P=I x D). The explanation explicitly downgrades competing distractors like differing stigma/awareness or sex distribution ('though A can be considered for a different class of disorders') — don't over-think this into a psychosocial explanation when a pure duration explanation is wanted.

bullets.text: Incidence = new cases / mid-interval at-risk population — a ratio against time, so 1-month incidence is always < 1-year incidence.
This is cumulative incidence — valid with low attrition, biased when attrition is high (dropouts excluded from the numerator, but denominator still includes them).
Incidence density (rate) = new cases per person-year, avoiding the attrition problem; compare groups via incidence rate ratios (unit-free).
Point prevalence = existing cases at one cross-sectional point / population at that point; period prevalence = same concept assessed over a period / mid-period population.
Prevalence = incidence × duration — chronic illness (e.g. schizophrenia) shows higher prevalence than acute illness (e.g. influenza) even at comparable incidence.

A vaccine lowers both incidence and prevalence; a cure lowers prevalence only (shorter duration, unchanged incidence); reduced mortality in chronic illness can raise prevalence via longevity without changing incidence.

sections.title: 3. Lifetime Prevalence vs Lifetime Morbid Risk

blocks.text: Lifetime prevalence = the proportion of individuals in the population who have ever manifested a disorder and are alive on a given day, ascertained by cross-sectional survey and recall of past status — this method is prone to recall bias.

Lifetime morbid risk (**LMR**) is the probability of a person developing the disorder across their entire life (often defined by the population's life expectancy) and must be distinguished from lifetime prevalence: **LMR** includes the whole birth cohort, past and future, including those already deceased at survey time. For low-incidence disorders such as schizophrenia, summing age-specific incidence rates gives an approximate **LMR** (Saha et al., 2004).

bullets.text: Lifetime prevalence = proportion ever having had a disorder, alive on a given day, via cross-sectional recall — prone to recall bias.

Lifetime morbid risk (**LMR**) = probability of developing the disorder across the whole life/birth cohort, including those already deceased. For low-incidence disorders (e.g. schizophrenia), **LMR** ≈ sum of age-specific incidence rates (Saha 2004).

blocks.text: Baseline prevalence = a disease's usual community level. Low-to-moderate baseline without significant fluctuation = endemic (most psychiatric disorders, with exceptions); a persistently **HIGH** baseline = hyperendemic; an irregular pattern of significant fluctuation from baseline = sporadic occurrence; occurrence that clearly **EXCEEDS** the expected level in a given time period = epidemic (can be a slow, steady rise as in multifactorial chronic disease, or an acute outbreak as in infectious disease); an epidemic of wide geographical proportion = pandemic (e.g. **HIV** pandemic).

expansion: Endemic: usual low-to-moderate baseline, no big fluctuation
Epidemic: occurrence clearly **EXCEEDS** the expected level for that time/place
Pandemic: an epidemic with wide **GEOGRAPHIC** spread

blocks.text: Distinguishing epidemic/pandemic/hyperendemic/endemic/sporadic: 'pandemic' is specifically defined by wide **GEOGRAPHICAL** spread, not by size of case numbers, level above baseline, or fluctuation pattern (those describe epidemic, hyperendemic and sporadic respectively) — don't pick hyperendemic or sporadic as distractors for 'wide geographical distribution'.

bullets.text: Baseline occurrence ladder: endemic (usual, no big fluctuation) → hyperendemic (persistently **HIGH**) → sporadic (irregular fluctuation) → epidemic (clearly **EXCEEDS** expected level) → pandemic (wide geographical spread, e.g. **HIV**).

blocks.text: A crude rate applies to the whole population (e.g. crude birth rate, crude mortality rate). A specific rate applies to a subgroup (e.g. age-specific, disease-specific, cause-specific mortality). A standardized rate applies observed rates to a hypothetical population adjusted for a variable (e.g. age), making rates from heterogeneous populations comparable — e.g. suicide rates in inner London are not directly comparable to rural Yorkshire because the working-age population differs and would spuriously inflate crude comparisons.

Cause-specific mortality rate = deaths due to a specific cause / total population size (e.g. alcohol-specific mortality). Case-fatality rate = deaths due to a specific disease / number of persons **AFFECTED** by that disease — a measure of the disease's fatal severity (e.g. 15 of 100 anorexia patients die of its complications).
Proportionate mortality rate = deaths due to a specific cause / total deaths in the population — a measure of that cause's contribution to overall societal mortality burden.

Years of Potential Life Lost (**YPLL**) sums, for deaths before a predetermined endpoint (usually age 65 or average life expectancy), the difference between that endpoint and age at death — this weights earlier deaths more heavily than later ones.

**DALY** (disability-adjusted life year) extends **YPLL** by adding equivalent years of healthy life lost to disability: **DALY** = **YLL** + **YLD**, where **YLL** = N x **LE** (N = number of deaths, **LE** = standard life expectancy at age of death) and **YLD** = I x **DW** x **LD** (I = number of incident cases, **DW** = disability weight, **LD** = average duration of the case until remission or death). One **DALY** = loss of one year of full health. **DALY** calculation applies ==3%== time discounting and non-uniform age weighting (less weight to years lived very young or very old).

Deaths due to a specific cause / total deaths in the population — measures that cause's contribution to overall mortality burden
Sum of (predetermined endpoint − age at death) for deaths before that endpoint; endpoint usually age 65 or average life expectancy; weights earlier deaths more heavily

blocks.forTopic: Crude vs specific vs standardized rates
blocks.mnemonic: Crude = whole Country, Specific = Subgroup, Standardized = Same hypothetical population
expansion: Crude rate: applies to the **WHOLE** population
Specific rate: applies to a **SUBGROUP** (age-, disease-, cause-specific)
Standardized rate: observed rates re-applied to a hypothetical, variable-adjusted population so different populations become comparable

blocks.title: Perinatal, neonatal and infant death definitions
rows: A liveborn infant who dies within 28 days
A liveborn infant who dies within 7 days
A liveborn infant who dies between 7 and 28 days
A fetus that dies before birth but after 24 weeks of gestation

expansion: Early neonatal death: liveborn dies within 7 days
Late neonatal death: liveborn dies between 7 and 28 days
Neonatal death (overall): liveborn dies within 28 days
Perinatal death = stillbirth (after 24 weeks gestation, before birth) + early neonatal death (within 7 days)

items.text: Infant death rate is **NOT** an example of a standardized/adjusted rate — restricting a sample to a subgroup (here, age <1 year) is merely a specific rate. Only the standardized mortality ratio is genuinely adjusted for a variable (e.g. age) **AFTER** observation.

Of the factors that can distort comparison between two crude mortality rates (socioeconomic stratification, ethnic composition, age distribution, gender distribution, population size), population **SIZE** is the one that does **NOT** matter — it is simply the denominator, whereas the others are genuine confounders of crude-rate comparisons.

Perinatal mortality (**WHO**) = stillbirths + deaths in the **FIRST** **WEEK** of life per 1,000 live births — do not confuse the 7-day cut-off here with the 28-day cut-off that defines overall neonatal death.

bullets.text: Crude rate = whole population; specific rate = subgroup (age-/disease-/cause-specific); standardized rate = observed rates re-applied to a hypothetical population adjusted for a variable (e.g. age) so heterogeneous populations become comparable — e.g. inner London vs rural Yorkshire suicide rates aren't directly comparable due to differing age structure.
Case-fatality rate = deaths from a disease / persons **AFFECTED** by it (fatal severity); cause-specific mortality rate = deaths from a cause / total population size.
Proportionate mortality rate = deaths from a cause / total deaths in the population — that cause's contribution to overall mortality burden.
**YPLL** sums (predetermined endpoint − age at death) for deaths before that endpoint (usually age 65 or life expectancy) — weights earlier deaths more heavily.
**DALY** = **YLL** + **YLD** (**YLL** = deaths × life expectancy at age of death; **YLD** = incident cases × disability weight × duration of case), plus non-uniform age weighting.

blocks.text: Bar charts represent each category of a variable as a bar whose length is proportional to the number of persons/events in that category. A frequency polygon plots the number of observations in each interval as a point at the interval's midpoint, then connects the points with straight lines.

A population pyramid portrays age and sex structure and reveals cohort trends over time. Three prototypical shapes (demographers): constrictive (fewer people in younger age bands, typical of countries like the **US** as birth rates fall after a baby boom), expansive (more people in younger age bands, typical of developing countries with high birth rates and short life expectancy from harsh conditions), and stationary (roughly equal numbers across age bands with tapering only at older ages, e.g. Sweden, from low constant birth rates and high quality of life).

bullets.text: Bar chart: bar length proportional to frequency per category. Frequency polygon: point plotted at each interval's midpoint, points joined by straight lines.

Population pyramid shows age/sex structure & cohort trends: constrictive (fewer young, e.g. **US** post-baby-boom), expansive (more young, developing countries), stationary (roughly equal across bands, tapering only at old age, e.g. Sweden).

sections.title: 7. History & Generations of Psychiatric Epidemiological Studies

blocks.text: First generation (~16 studies, pre-**WWII**, includes the Midtown Manhattan study): focused on health-care-agency-registered prevalence of mental disorder in relation to community characteristics.

Second generation (post-**WWII**, ~60 studies): increased interest in diagnostic criteria/classification/nomenclature; largely field surveys using unstructured clinical interviews, so reliability was low.

Third generation (from ~1970): major effort to increase diagnostic reliability, aiming for precise prevalence/incidence estimates of **SPECIFIC** disorders — contrasted with the second generation's focus on mental ill-health in general.

A claimed fourth generation incorporates comprehensive biologic markers (brain imaging, **CSF** examination, blood sampling) into large-scale cross-sectional surveys, e.g. the **H70** study (Skoog, 2004).

bullets.text: 1st generation (~16 studies, pre-**WWII**, e.g. Midtown Manhattan): health-care-registered prevalence vs community characteristics.
2nd generation (post-**WWII**, ~60 studies): shift to diagnostic criteria/classification, but relied on unstructured clinical interviews → low reliability.
3rd generation (from ~1970): raised diagnostic reliability to estimate prevalence/incidence of **SPECIFIC** disorders (vs 2nd generation's general mental-ill-health focus).
Claimed 4th generation adds biologic markers (imaging, **CSF**, blood) to large cross-sectional surveys, e.g. the **H70** study (Skoog, 2004).

sections.title: 8. Disorder Burden & Sex Ratios (ESEMED / SPMM Epidemiological Data)

blocks.text: **ESEMED** epidemiological study: ==1 in 4== adults has a lifetime mental disorder; ==1 in 10== has one in the last year. Lifetime mood disorder ==14.7%== (major depression alone ==13%==); lifetime anxiety ==14%== (specific phobia alone ==8%==); lifetime alcohol use disorder ==5.2%==.

Sex-ratio caveats worth remembering: several 'higher in one sex' ratios narrow or equalise specifically in treatment-seeking samples (social phobia, **OCD**); Alzheimer's 2:1 female excess in prevalence may reflect female longevity rather than a true incidence difference; pre-puberty major depression runs marginally **MORE** common in boys, reversing to the well-known 2:1 female excess only after puberty.
Schizophrenia's 1.4:1 male excess (Saha et al., PLoS Med 2004) is for **INCIDENCE** only — prevalence is roughly equal between sexes.

blocks.title: Disorders with Higher Female Preponderance
rows: Social phobia (may be equal in treatment-seekers)
Alzheimer's disease (prevalence; incidence may be equal)
Major depression (post-puberty; pre-puberty boys marginally > girls)

blocks.title: Disorders with Higher Male Preponderance

bullets.text: Sex ratios narrow in treatment-seeking samples (social phobia, **OCD**); schizophrenia's 1.4:1 male excess is incidence-only (prevalence roughly equal); Alzheimer's 2:1 female excess in prevalence may reflect longevity, not incidence; pre-puberty **MDD** is marginally **MORE** common in boys, reversing to the well-known female excess only post-puberty.

sections.title: 9. Levels of Prevention (question-bank only — not covered in the book notes for this topic)

blocks.note: Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: Primary prevention averts the illness/epidemic before it occurs (e.g. public health initiatives such as poverty eradication or a healthy diet; vaccination to pre-empt an illness, e.g. flu vaccination reducing post-influenza depression). Secondary prevention targets high-risk groups for early detection/treatment (e.g. early intervention services in psychosis). Tertiary prevention reduces disability and progression once a disorder is clinically established, including rehabilitation.

Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: Because current knowledge of psychiatric risk factors and causal insults is limited, tertiary prevention is the level most commonly employed in current psychiatric practice.

Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: Continuous treatment aimed at giving chronic patients their best-attainable quality of life/functioning is **TERTIARY** prevention, not secondary prevention.

blocks.text: 'Continuous treatment to enable chronic patients to attain best quality of life' sounds like ongoing (secondary) care but is classified as **TERTIARY** prevention — a frequently confused level pairing in 'except' style questions.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: Tertiary prevention specifically means preventing progression of an already-established disease and reducing the resulting disability once diagnosis is well established (e.g. encouraging a patient with schizophrenia's negative symptoms to attend a day centre to reduce disability).

expansion: Primary = Prevent occurrence (vaccination, public health measures)
Secondary = Pick-up early in high-risk groups (screening, early intervention)
Tertiary = Patch-up: reduce disability and rehabilitate once disease is established

sections.title: 10. Pathways to Care, Ecological Fallacy & Deprivation Indices (question-bank only — not covered in the book notes for this topic)

blocks.note: Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: The pathways-of-care (filter) model, proposed by Goldberg, explains the difference in prevalence rates seen across settings from the community up to tertiary care centres, via a series of sequential filters. The **FIRST** filter between disease and healthcare delivery is recognition of symptoms by the patient (self-recognition) — illness behaviour, which varies widely even between people with the same illness severity, is the strong determinant at this first stage.

blocks.text: In Goldberg's pathways-of-care (filter) model, the **FIRST** filter between disease and secondary psychiatric care is the patient's own recognition of symptoms (self-recognition), driven by illness behaviour — not **GP** recognition (second stage) and not availability of hospital beds or community services (later stages). Illness behaviour is specifically tested as the determinant **AT** **THIS** **FIRST** **STAGE**.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: Ecological fallacy: an inference error made when a researcher attributes an individual-level cause to an individual based on aggregate/group-level data (e.g. concluding that psychiatrists themselves 'drive' patients to suicide because areas with more consultant psychiatrists per catchment population show higher suicide rates).

blocks.text: Inferring that consultant psychiatrists 'drive' patients to suicide because catchment areas with more psychiatrists per population show higher suicide rates is the **ECOLOGICAL** **FALLACY** (an individual-level causal claim drawn from aggregate/group-level data) — not selection bias, measurement bias, sampling error, or a type 2 error, all of which are plausible-sounding distractors.

blocks.note: Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: The Jarman index (Brian Jarman) is a scoring system for relative social deprivation in a community, derived from census data (percentages of elderly living alone, single-parent families, under-5s, unskilled/unemployed persons, ethnic minorities, overcrowded dwellings, recent address changes, etc.). It is a valid indicator but not generally accepted outside the **UK**.

Not covered in books/14-epidemiology.pdf or books/7-0-epidemiological-data.pdf — tested via the question bank: Attack rate is simply an incidence rate following an acute exposure: number of cases that develop / number exposed (at risk) in the cohort.

blocks.text: Attack rate denominator trap: it is the **ORIGINAL** number exposed/at-risk in the cohort, not the number of survivors at follow-up and not a figure adjusted for interim deaths — e.g. 50 cases from 1500 originally exposed gives an attack rate of 50/1500, not 50/1450 or 38/1500.

blocks.subtopic: Levels of prevention (primary/secondary/tertiary) and Goldberg's pathways-of-care/filter model
